idiom_name: hand-written step-function chain: struct of function pointers + void *context, driven by one loop
implementation_notes: The C standard library has no closures, generics or reduction protocol, so the transducer form must be built by hand out of the type-erasure idiom the library itself uses: a step function with a void *context parameter (qsort's comparator, qsort_s's context, BSD's qsort_r) packaged into a struct that also carries the stage's captured parameters and a pointer to the downstream reducer. A transducer is then a function taking a Reducer and returning a Reducer, composed by nesting, and the driver is a single for loop that stops as soon as a step reports 'done' - the C analogue of Clojure's Reduced. Nothing in the language replaces the classic structure here; what a hand-written fused loop still does better is type safety and speed, so the callback chain only pays off when several sources and sinks must share the same stage or when the transformation set is assembled at runtime from a table of function pointers.
pitfalls: The context structs are the stage state: a compound literal or stack local bound into a pipeline dies at scope end, and the pipeline then dereferences freed memory (the same lifetime trap as returning a C iterator built from a compound literal).

void * erases the element type: qsort-style callbacks receive a pointer to the buffer slot, so a stage silently accepts a mismatched element type (T where T* was meant) and the compiler cannot check that a map A->B feeds a stage expecting B.
Without an explicit stop signal the driver cannot short-circuit, so take/drop stages keep pulling the source until it is exhausted.
